newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian candidate said concussed after attack.
newsitem.headline: Croatian candidate said concussed after attack.

text.p: Vlado Gotovac, one of two challengers to Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in next week's presidential election, is suffering from concussion after being struck on the head at a rally, party officials said on Friday.

Gotovac was due to be flown to a Zagreb hospital for medical checks by helicopter, but the flight was delayed due to bad weather. He will arrive later on a military plane, officials of the Croatian Social Liberal Party (HSLS) said.
The 66-year-old candidate was struck with a belt buckle by a man wearing Croatian army uniform at a rally in the town of Pula on the Istrian peninsula late on Thursday.
Describing Gotovac's injuries as serious, his party accused the state media of downplaying their nature and said he was suffering from concussion and shock.

"This morning his condition worsened. Haematoma is spreading on the left part of the head, his left eye is closing. He can't get up due to dizziness," party secretary Karl Gorinsek told a news conference. Another official said the injuries could have been fatal.

The defence ministry named the attacker as Croatian army captain Tomislav Brzovic and said he had been immediately suspended from duty and detained, state news agency HINA reported. It said the soldier was drunk.

"The defence ministry most energetically condemns this violent act and will undertake serious measures to prevent similar incidents in the future," the ministry told HINA, adding criminal charges were pressed against the attacker.

Brzovic struck Gotovac on the head from behind after which Gotovac fell to the ground, the HSLS said in a statement read to journalists. It said no police reacted until the enraged crowd tried to catch Brzovic who had been pushed from the stage by the party's head of security.
Last week protesters stoned a small blue van in which the other opposition candidate, Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democrats, is campaiging around Croatia.
Gotovac and Tomac are fighting an uphill battle to try and oust Tudjman who is expected to win outright on June 15, with between 60 and 70 percent of the votes in the first round.
They are touring the country in a frenetic dash to convince voters it is time to change Croatia's autocratic government.

"Running at these elections is a gesture aimed to show against all the odds that there is another Croatia which resists the present ruling style...and that there are people who are displeased with it," Gotovac told Reuters in a recent interview.
Only hours before the attack, the government decreed that all presidential candidates must be afforded full security during the pre-election campaign.
The opposition leaders blamed the attack on the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) and the state media which, they said, had created a mood of fear and intolerance.

"Tudjman, his HDZ party and Croatian state television systematically satanise all the opposition leaders, feeding the idea that they are enemies of the state," said Zlatko Tomcic of the Peasant Party, which is backing Gotovac's campaign.
"In the uninformed part of the population this falls on fertile ground and awakens base passions," he added.
The HDZ on Friday condemned the incident.

"We hope Mr Gotovac will continue his campaign without problems. Unfortunately, such incidents cannot be ruled out but we hope they will not be repeated," Ivic Pasalic, the head of Tudjman's electoral team, told a news conference.
Gotovac's party said he was sure to run in the elections, although some campaign rallies will have to be cancelled.
